strand_a.title: In geoeconomic times, EU trade and industry should remain sources of creation toward reglobalisation
strand_a.summary: In geoeconomic times, EU trade and industry should remain sources of creation toward reglobalisation. Abstract In apical geoeconomic times, the EU – whose economy relies heavily on trade openness – sees its economic competitiveness and resilience being structurally eroded. To continue taking advantage of the benefits of a more integrated single market – with an outward-looking industrial policy and facilitated intra-EU trade – as well as of open trade as adjusted to strategic autonomy, it is crucial for the EU to continue conceiving trade and industry as sources of preservation and – critically – also of creation for the longer term driven by reglobalisation.

strand_a.title: The quest for European autonomy and the risks of EU and NATO precarity
strand_a.summary: While Europe has long debated the need for greater strategic autonomy, recent crises and the U.S.’s partial disengagement from European security have intensified expectations for Europeans to assume more responsibility on security and defense. However, the collective European rights and resources within these existing organizations have not kept pace creating a paradox: as the EU and NATO have expanded their roles on matters related to European security, they have experienced increased precarity, failing to deliver on transformative resilience toward a more autonomous Europe. strand_a.title: Design global, manufacture local: operationalizing post-growth industrial policy through cosmolocalism
strand_a.summary: The resurgence of industrial policy across advanced economies responds to ecological, geopolitical, and socio-economic crises, yet existing frameworks remain contradictory: while seeking resilience, strategic autonomy, and sustainability, they maintain structural dependencies on growth driving ecological overshoot and resource conflicts. Design global, manufacture local: operationalizing post-growth industrial policy through cosmolocalism. This article demonstrates how cosmolocalism – circulating knowledge as global commons while maintaining local material production – can help operationalize post-growth industrial policy across three pillars: foundational liveability, peaceful planetary co-existence, and democratically coordinated sustainability.

strand_a.summary: Operationalising Circularity: Legal, Technical, and Governance Dimensions of Digital Product Passports in EU Construction Procurement. Digital Product Passports (DPPs) are increasingly promoted as a key mechanism to support this transition, as they provide product-specific data on material composition, environmental performance, repairability and end-of-life pathways, enabling procurement decisions based on lifecycle considerations rather than price alone. strand_a.title: Canada: Off the Menu?
strand_a.summary: In his second term, US President Donald Trump has deployed against Canada the same coercive toolkit that Russia has used against its neighbours: economic coercion, annexationist rhetoric and support for internal separatist movements. Post-Soviet states responded to Russian pressure by diversifying their dependencies, and Canada is now doing the same: joining European Union defence-procurement efforts, ordering submarines from Germany, and signing trade agreements across Asia and Europe. Russia’s coercion was designed to keep its neighbours inside its sphere of influence, but instead accelerated their departure.

strand_a.authors: Sandra Eckert, Lucas Seghezzo, Cristian Darío Venencia, Carlos Ortega Insaurralde, Louis Zwyssig, Gabi Sonderegger, M Giger
strand_a.summary: We find that domestic investors account for the majority (54.7%) of the acquired soy-producing land, with foreign investors from the US (15.4%), the EU (5.6%), and the Gulf region (4.6%) playing smaller roles. The EU accounts for a considerable share of trade (16.2%) and a moderate share of investment (5.6%).

strand_a.title: Government as a Strategic Actor: A Framework for Assessing Regulatory Risk in Digital Markets
strand_a.summary: This paper argues that effective risk assessment requires moving beyond a static view of government as a rule‐maker to analyzing it as a dynamic, strategic actor. We develop a tripartite framework that enables managers to evaluate regulatory risk by analyzing a state's discursive commitments (public narratives and policy signals), institutional capacity (administrative design and enforcement power), and material leverage (control over key technological infrastructure). Applied to the landmark European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, the framework reveals critical “orchestration gaps” between a state's regulatory ambitions and its infrastructural dependencies.

strand_a.title: Shifting paths? The evolution of Southern European growth trajectories in the post-Eurozone crisis decade (2010–9)
strand_a.authors: Fabio Bulfone, Mischa Stratenwerth, Arianna Tassinari
strand_a.summary: The evolution of Southern European growth trajectories in the post-Eurozone crisis decade (2010–9). Abstract This article traces the growth trajectories of Southern European economies (Greece, Italy, Portugal, and Spain) over the decade 2010–9. Our results show that Southern European economies share important similarities: export-led growth has been insufficient to boost aggregate growth, stimulate high value-added exports, reverse pro-cyclical employment declines, or create high-wage employment opportunities.

strand_a.title: Accelerating fossil gas independence in Europe
strand_a.authors: Lukas Franken, Iegor Riepin, T H Brown
strand_a.summary: Recent price shocks have prompted calls to curb Europe's dependence on fossil gas imports, but the cost of this goal, and the consumer protection it affords, remain uncertain. Here we address this gap by imposing constraints on fossil gas supply in a European energy system model that co-optimises abatement across all gas uses at high spatio-temporal resolution. Cutting import reliance proves economically compelling: through savings in power generation and low-temperature heat in industry and buildings, Europe can halve its natural gas consumption for 16bnEUR/a, aligning demand with the continent's production capacity of 200 bcm.

strand_a.title: Cold War 2.0 and defence readiness

As a worst case, we investigate the trade channel of geo-economic fragmentation in a Cold War 2.0 implying a complete cessation of trade with CRINK and a full blockade of Taiwan in an international multi-sectoral macroeconomic model featuring the defence sector and interlinking countries via global supply chains. Even this less kinetic conflict will create challenges for Europe’s security—challenges that will only grow more acute as the crisis worsens.

strand_a.title: The role of green hydrogen imports under demand and supply uncertainties in Europe
strand_a.authors: Frederik Dahl Nielsen, Stian Backe, Benjamin Mitterrutzner, Pedro Crespo del Granado
strand_a.summary: To achieve climate neutrality, Europe’s hydrogen strategy combines domestic green hydrogen production with green hydrogen imports, but the optimal balance remains uncertain. This study applies the stochastic energy system model EMPIRE, coupled with sectoral demand projections, to quantify how variable renewable energy source (VRES) deployment trajectories and hydrogen demand pathways jointly shape Europe’s import requirements. Results show that import requirements in 2050 could range from 7.5 to 55 Mton/yr, depending on scenario developments.

page_guarantee.rule: New records update candidate reasoning; the shelf is re-decided each scan from recomputed maturity. No record takes a slot automatically.
page_guarantee.creative_reserve: Reserve = grounded runners-up + a creative reserve of relevant, uncontradicted hypotheses (distant, cross-domain, emerging, weak-signal or partially grounded), at least 18 and topped up toward 45, rotated across wow levels with weight on surprise. They mature into page competition when grounded.

high_order_inference.publication_policy: Stage 7 claim-native selection treats the reasoning layer as a future-hypothesis corpus. Candidate formation is broad; missing roles, thin evidence and unrun counter-evidence tests lower maturity rather than forbidding the hypothesis. Grounded candidates compete only within their wow 1-5 bucket. Each product reserves three public slots per wow level (15 total), displayed 5-4-3-2-1 three times; surplus grounded findings remain reserve and weaker hypotheses remain developing.
high_order_inference.lifecycle_policy: Claim-native stock persists as page/reserve/developing tiers. Evidence is recomputed each scan; candidates can strengthen, weaken or move between tiers as new evidence arrives. Counter-evidence and falsifier results affect maturity and can kill a contradicted hypothesis, but an unrun challenge is not a ban on future-facing reasoning.
high_order_inference.candidate_search_policy: Missing-role and falsifier queries remain ordinary scanner discovery inputs and receive no admission waiver.

Securing extractive futures: unpacking the EU’s Critical Raw Materials Act. In 2024 the European Union’s (EU’s) Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) entered into force, seeking to ensure access to a secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials (CRMs).
